title: Sebastian (20 January)
hookLine: a soldier-martyr painted pierced with arrows, who in his story survives them; patron of athletes

lines: A YOUNG MAN AND THE ARROWS.
cards: In a gallery of old paintings, a young man looks back at you, tied to a tree or a column, calm, with arrows standing out of his body. It's easy to assume you're looking at the moment he died. In his story, you aren't.
The arrows are the part he survived. His name is Sebastian, and he ends a week of saints from the calendar's first weeks of January.

teach.h: A REAL MARTYR, A LATER LEGEND.
teach.b: Very little about Sebastian is certain. Saint Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, mentions him as a martyr from Milan who died in Rome.
The full story comes from a much later account, and here is the story it tells, the one the Church has handed down.
Sebastian was an officer in the emperor's guard and quietly a Christian. He used his post to visit Christians in prison and keep their courage up.
When he was found out, the emperor had him tied up and shot with arrows by his own fellow soldiers, and left for dead.
A Christian widow named Irene came at night to take his body for burial, and found him breathing. She took him home and nursed him. Then the turn.
Healed, Sebastian did not leave Rome.

teach.h: HE GOES BACK TO THE EMPEROR.
teach.b: He stood where the emperor would pass and told him to his face that he was wrong to persecute Christians. This time he was beaten to death.

Tradition honors him as a patron of athletes and soldiers, and some readers see why: a body that took the blow and got back up. Some hear in him Paul's words near the end of his second letter to Timothy.
In the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith."

Look back at this week: Genevieve calming Paris, Kuriakose Chavara putting a school beside a church, André the doorkeeper, Marguerite teaching in a stable, Hilary refusing to sign, Anthony walking into the desert.

how: Catholics keep Saint Sebastian's memorial in January, and sports clubs, athletes and soldiers in various places honor him as a patron.

games.q: you're Sebastian. you survived the arrows and Irene has nursed you back to health. the emperor thinks you're dead. what do you do?
o: slip out of Rome and live quietly somewhere else.
go and stand where the emperor will pass.
games.why: in the story he confronted the emperor about persecuting Christians, and was beaten to death.

practice: Bring to mind someone who trains their body: a kid at Saturday soccer, a friend who runs before work, someone learning to walk again after an injury. Picture them in the last stretch, the moment they want to stop.
If you pray, ask Sebastian to pray for them; if you don't, wish them strength and a safe body, one name at a time.

wordCard.voice: Sebastian. A soldier-martyr of Rome. In his story he survived the arrows, was nursed by Irene, and went back to face the emperor.

orig.note: Latin: his name as the Roman calendar keeps it.

carryVoice: Your line: arrows didn't stop him. Irene's care got him back on his feet. Day nine hundred fifty-nine, done.
